summary: On 24 February 2008 Pakistan Telecom announced a more-specific route for a YouTube prefix, intending to block YouTube inside Pakistan. Its upstream propagated the route and YouTube's traffic was drawn to Pakistan for about two hours.

overview.background: BGP routes are trusted between networks and a longer prefix wins. Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced a /24 inside YouTube's /22. Its upstream PCCW Global (AS3491) propagated it.
overview.impact: Traffic for YouTube was drawn to Pakistan Telecom for about 2 hours 14 minutes.
overview.severity: A global service disruption that lasted from 18:47 to 21:01 UTC.
overview.gaps: The page's IP addresses were stripped when it was read, so prefixes are described by length only.

diagrams.title: A more-specific announcement wins
diagrams.caption: RIPE NCC's case study shows the hijacked /24 was seen by 105 peers against the legitimate /22 seen by 112.

diagrams.title: Origin validation and customer filtering (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Controls that would reject this route. Not part of RIPE NCC's case study.

afterChanges: Customers announce only what they own.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: AS17557 begins announcing the prefix, propagated by AS3491.
YouTube begins announcing the prefix from AS36561.
YouTube announces more-specific prefixes, which win on longest-prefix match.
Pakistan Telecom's announcements appear with extra prepending, so more routers prefer YouTube's route.
AS3491 withdraws all prefixes originated by AS17557, ending the hijack.
The last unauthorised announcement from Pakistan is received.

rootCause.trigger: Pakistan Telecom announced a prefix it did not own.
rootCause.underlying: A longer prefix wins in BGP and the upstream propagated the announcement.
contributing: No prefix filter at the upstream
No origin validation at the time
Routers prefer longer prefixes by design

evidence.label: Start of the hijack
evidence.body: Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) started an unauthorised announcement of the prefix
evidence.note: From the RIPE NCC case study.

evidence.label: End of the hijack
evidence.body: withdraws all prefixes originated by AS17557 (Pakistan Telecom), thus stopping the hijack

evidence.label: A simulated lookup
evidence.note: How a present-day lookup on an AS could be made. Not 2008 data.

diagnose.step: Look at BGP for the prefix.

verify.step: Check routes return to the legitimate origin.

fix.safety: Announcing more-specific prefixes can leak traffic or increase the routing table. Use it as a short-term response only.

troubleshoot.scenario: Part of the internet cannot reach your service. Route collectors show a longer prefix from an unknown origin.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
hints: How do you regain traffic quickly?
troubleshoot.answer: Announce the same or more-specific prefixes, contact the upstream and origin, then use ROAs and monitoring.

rootcause.q: How long did the unauthorised announcement last?

remediation.answer: Alert on new origin AS for your prefixes.

design.answer: ROAs, route collector monitoring, defined contacts and a playbook for more-specific announcements.

checks.q: Which AS was the legitimate origin?

sources.title: RIPE NCC: YouTube Hijacking: A RIPE NCC RIS case study
